city.name: Charles Town
summary: Charles Town was the richest city in the colonies, and the fourth largest, with about 12,000 people in 1775, more than half of them enslaved. Rice and indigo grown by enslaved Africans on the Lowcountry plantations went out over its wharves, and its merchants and planters built fine brick houses and churches between the Ashley and Cooper rivers.

In June 1776 a British fleet attacked the harbour and was beaten off by a palmetto-log fort on Sullivan's Island. The British came back in 1780. Clinton's army landed south of the town, crossed the Ashley and dug its way down the Neck towards the American lines. On 12 May 1780 General Lincoln surrendered the town and his whole army, about 5,000 men: the worst American defeat of the war.
city.note: Streets, the hornwork and the American lines, and buildings standing in 1780 from OpenHistoricalMap (CC0). OpenHistoricalMap has no historic shoreline here, so the coast is the modern one from OpenStreetMap, with the town's shore drawn by hand where it has since been filled: the Battery, the Cooper waterfront, the Ashley marshes and the creek under Market Street. The wharves and British parallels are placed by hand after period plans of the siege, so their exact lines are approximate. Houses between the streets are generated.

properties.name: St Michael's Church
description: Built from 1752 and opened in 1761 at the crossing of Broad and Meeting streets. Its white steeple, 186 feet high, was the town's landmark from the sea, During the war the Americans painted it black to hide it from British gunners. It only stood out more.
When the British left in 1782 they took its bells to London as a prize. A merchant bought them and sent them back.
properties.wiki: St. Michael's Episcopal Church (Charleston, South Carolina)

properties.name: St Philip's Church
description: The mother church of the colony, built of brick and stucco in the 1710s and 1720s. It stood out into Church Street, which still bends round its site.
That church burned in 1835. The present St Philip's was built on the same spot.

properties.name: Exchange and Custom House
description: Built in 1767 to 1771 at the foot of Broad Street, facing the harbour, where ships' cargoes were taxed and merchants met. In 1774 South Carolina's patriots met here to choose delegates to the First Continental Congress.
After the surrender the British used its cellar as a prison for patriots, the Provost Dungeon.

properties.name: Statehouse
description: The colony's Statehouse, built from 1753 at the crossing of Broad and Meeting streets, across from St Michael's. The royal governor, his council and the assembly met here, and from 1776 the government of independent South Carolina.
It burned in 1788. The courthouse that stands here now was built on its walls.

properties.name: Powder Magazine
description: A squat brick store for the town's gunpowder, built in 1713. It is the oldest public building in South Carolina.

properties.name: Miles Brewton House
description: One of the grandest town houses in America, built about 1769 for the slave trader and merchant Miles Brewton. After the town fell, British commanders made it their headquarters: Sir Henry Clinton, then Lord Rawdon and Lord Cornwallis.

properties.name: Heyward-Washington House
description: The brick house of Thomas Heyward Jr., built in 1772. Heyward signed the Declaration of Independence. He fought in the militia, was taken prisoner when the town fell, and was shipped to St Augustine.

properties.name: Broughton's Battery
description: A gun battery on White Point, the southern tip of the town, guarding the harbour since the early 1700s.

properties.name: Cooper River wharves
description: Private wharves ran out from the Bay, the waterfront street, into the Cooper River. Rice, indigo and deerskins went out over them to Britain, and ships brought in manufactured goods and enslaved Africans. Charles Town was the busiest slave port in North America.

properties.name: Gadsden's Wharf
description: Christopher Gadsden, the patriot merchant, built this wharf from 1767. At about 840 feet it was the longest in America. Gadsden was lieutenant governor in 1780; he urged Lincoln to hold the town, and in the end to give it up.
From 1803 to 1808 it was the main landing place for enslaved Africans brought into the United States. The International African American Museum stands on the site.

properties.name: The Hornwork
description: A fort of tabby, a concrete of lime and oyster shell, built from 1757 across the road out of town. In 1780 it was the strong point at the centre of the American lines.
A fragment of its wall survives in Marion Square.

properties.name: American lines
description: Earth walls and gun batteries across the Neck, from the Ashley marshes to the Cooper, rebuilt in 1779 and 1780 round the old hornwork. In front lay a flooded ditch, the canal, and rows of sharpened logs.
Behind them General Benjamin Lincoln held about 5,000 Continentals, militia and sailors. Once British troops crossed the Cooper River in April, there was no way out.

properties.name: The canal
description: A wet ditch dug across the Neck in early 1780 in front of the American lines. The British sapped up to it in early May and drained it.

properties.name: British first parallel
description: Clinton's engineers broke ground on the night of 1 April 1780, about 800 yards from the American lines, near the village of Hampstead. Within days this trench was armed with batteries, which opened fire on 13 April.

properties.name: British second parallel
description: Dug in the middle of April, about halfway to the American lines, joined to the first by zigzag approach trenches.

properties.name: British third parallel
description: Pushed to within about a hundred yards of the canal in early May. From here the British drained the ditch and could storm the lines, and on 11 May they fired heated shot into the town. Lincoln surrendered the next day.

properties.name: British battery
description: Gun batteries dug into the first parallel. They opened fire on the American lines and the town on 13 April 1780.

properties.name: Harleston Village
description: A new suburb laid out in 1770 on the marshy Ashley side of town. By 1780 it had streets but only scattered houses and gardens.

properties.name: Fort Sullivan (Fort Moultrie)
description: A square fort of palmetto logs and sand on Sullivan's Island, still unfinished when a British fleet attacked it on 28 June 1776. The soft palmetto wood swallowed the cannonballs. William Moultrie's guns badly damaged the ships, and the fleet sailed away.
The fort was named after him. In 1780 the British fleet ran past its guns on 8 April, and its garrison surrendered on 7 May. The fort there now is a later one.

properties.name: Fort Johnson
description: The old royal fort on James Island, across the harbour from the town. South Carolina militia seized it in September 1775. In 1780 the Americans gave it up as the British closed in.

properties.name: Hampstead
description: A suburb laid out in 1769 on the Neck, still mostly fields. The British dug their siege lines and batteries here.

properties.name: Liberty Tree
description: A live oak in a pasture north of town, where the Sons of Liberty met from 1766 and where the Declaration of Independence was read in August 1776. The British cut it down after they took the town.
